images.title: Count white, count black
images.purpose: Recap the colouring check: every 2 × 1 tile covers one white and one black square, so unequal counts mean no tiling.
images.composition: A chessboard coloured region on the left, one example tile in the middle and a short tally on the right, with plenty of white space.
exact_structure: Left: a 4 × 4 grid coloured like a chessboard, with the top left square white; black squares filled dark (#2B2B2B), white squares white with grey (#6B7280) outlines.
Two white squares are removed and drawn as dashed empty outlines: row 1, column 1 and row 3, column 3.
So exactly 14 squares remain: 6 white and 8 black.
In the middle: one separate 2 × 1 tile, one half white and one half black, outlined in reddish purple (#CC79A7), with the caption 1 white + 1 black.
Right: a tally of two lines, white 6 and black 8, followed by one line 6 ≠ 8 in vermilion (#D55E00).
rejection: remaining counts other than 6 white and 8 black, or two neighbouring squares of the same colour
removed squares in positions other than row 1 column 1 and row 3 column 3
the example tile showing two squares of the same colour
images.takeaway: Before tiling, count white and black squares: if they are unequal, the region cannot be tiled.
images.description: A 4 by 4 chessboard with two white squares removed, a black and white example tile, and the tally white 6, black 8, 6 ≠ 8.
images.context: Shown beside the practice concept on counting colours before tiling, before the student uses the colour count tool.
images.teaching_notes: Let students count the white and black squares themselves before reading the tally, then explain why each tile uses one of each.

image_decisions.why: A coloured board with a tally recaps the black and white counting check before practice.
